about: The strategy cards for /arena. Every competitor gets the same task and exactly one card: one reasoning mode, one workflow, one strategy. 15 x 12 x 12 = 2,160 distinct cards. bracket.py deals them with no repeats and spreads them evenly, so a 100-agent arena uses every reasoning mode, every workflow and every strategy. Edit freely: add an entry and the dealer picks it up. Ids must stay unique within a list.

reasoning.name: First principles
reasoning.how: Strip the task down to the facts and requirements nobody can argue with. Rebuild the answer from those alone, and keep a convention only if it earns its place again.

reasoning.name: Inversion
reasoning.how: Ask what would make this answer fail. List every way it could, then build the answer that makes each of those failures impossible.

reasoning.name: Analogy
reasoning.how: Find a problem in a different field that has already been solved and has the same shape. Port its solution over, then fix every place where the analogy breaks.

reasoning.name: Adversarial
reasoning.how: Picture the harshest expert reviewer trying to tear the answer apart. Write their attacks down first and build the answer backwards from them.

reasoning.name: Constraint first
reasoning.how: List every hard constraint, stated and implied: time, budget, tools, format, audience, platform. Solve strictly inside that box and let the tightest constraint drive the design.

reasoning.name: Worked example
reasoning.how: Solve one concrete, realistic instance end to end first, with real values. Generalise only from what that example actually taught you.

reasoning.name: Socratic
reasoning.how: Interrogate the task with the questions a sharp expert would ask before starting. Answer each one explicitly and let the answers decide the shape of the solution.

reasoning.name: Contrarian
reasoning.how: Write down the obvious default answer, then argue seriously against it. Keep only what survives the argument, even if that takes you the unpopular way.

reasoning.name: Systems thinking
reasoning.how: Map the moving parts, how they affect each other, and what happens second and third order. Optimise the whole system, not just the one part the task points at.

reasoning.name: Decomposition
reasoning.how: Break the task into independent sub-problems. Solve each one completely, then integrate them and test the seams where they meet.

reasoning.name: Working backwards
reasoning.how: Describe the finished result precisely, as if it already exists. Then work backwards, step by step, to where the user is right now.

reasoning.name: Probabilistic
reasoning.how: Treat every claim and choice as uncertain. Weigh what is likely, prefer what holds up across most scenarios, and state your confidence where it changes the decision.

reasoning.name: Dialectical
reasoning.how: State the strongest version of one answer, then the strongest opposing answer, then write the synthesis that keeps what is true in both.

reasoning.name: Evidence first
reasoning.how: Ground every claim in something checkable: the task text, the files it points to, the numbers given, documentation. Anything you cannot check gets labelled as an assumption.

reasoning.name: Expert panel
reasoning.how: Answer the task as three different experts would, picking roles that fit it. Take the strongest idea from each and settle every point where they disagree.

workflows.name: Draft, critique, rewrite
workflows.how: Write a complete first draft. Critique it line by line against the task as if someone else wrote it. Then rewrite it from scratch using the critique.

workflows.name: Outline first
workflows.how: Write a skeleton outline, check the outline against every requirement in the task, fix it, and only then fill it in.

workflows.name: Test first
workflows.how: Before writing the answer, write the checks it must pass: acceptance tests for code, pass or fail criteria for anything else. Then write the answer and run every check against it.

workflows.name: Research, then synthesise
workflows.how: Gather every relevant fact first: the task, any files or context it points to, what is known about the domain. Write nothing until the research is done, then synthesise.

workflows.name: Three drafts, pick one
workflows.how: Write three short, genuinely different approaches. Pick the strongest on the task's own terms and develop only that one fully.

workflows.name: Requirements checklist
workflows.how: Pull every requirement out of the task into a numbered list. Solve, then tick each item off and say exactly where it is met.

workflows.name: Iterative deepening
workflows.how: Write a one-paragraph answer first. Then expand the parts that matter most in two more passes, each one deeper than the last.

workflows.name: Build, then break
workflows.how: Build the answer. Then throw five hostile inputs or scenarios at it, write down what breaks, and patch every break.

workflows.name: Smallest version first
workflows.how: Produce the smallest complete version that actually works. Then extend it one step at a time, keeping it working after every step.

workflows.name: Options matrix
workflows.how: List the realistic options, score them in a small matrix against the criteria that matter for this task, choose one, and write up the choice.

workflows.name: Open questions first
workflows.how: List every open question the task leaves. Resolve each one with reasoning or a stated assumption, then answer.

workflows.name: Write, then restructure
workflows.how: Write freely and fast. Then outline what you actually wrote, fix the structure, and rewrite it to the new outline.

strategies.name: Simplest thing that works
strategies.how: Pick the least complicated answer that fully does the job. Every extra part has to justify itself.

strategies.name: Maximal rigour
strategies.how: Be exhaustive and exact. Check every step, verify every claim, and leave no hand-waving anywhere.

strategies.name: User empathy first
strategies.how: Start from the person who will use this: their situation, their skill level, and what they will actually do next. Shape everything around that.

strategies.name: Edge cases first
strategies.how: Hunt the edge cases, failure modes and weird inputs first, and design the answer around surviving them.

strategies.name: Speed
strategies.how: Optimise for the fastest route to something usable today. Cut anything that does not move the result.

strategies.name: Defensive
strategies.how: Assume the inputs are bad and the conditions are hostile. Make the answer fail safely and loudly rather than quietly.

strategies.name: Clarity above all
strategies.how: Make it the easiest answer to read and act on: plain words, obvious structure, nothing the reader has to decode.

strategies.name: Completeness
strategies.how: Leave out nothing the task asks for or clearly implies. Cover every requirement explicitly.

strategies.name: Fewest moving parts
strategies.how: Remove things until it breaks, then put the last one back. Fewer steps, fewer dependencies, fewer words.

strategies.name: Explicit trade-offs
strategies.how: Name the real trade-offs, choose for the user's most likely constraints, and say plainly what that choice gives up.

strategies.name: Built to last
strategies.how: Optimise for how this holds up in six months: easy to maintain, easy to extend, no traps for the next person.

strategies.name: Concrete specifics
strategies.how: Exact numbers, names, commands, file paths and steps. Zero generic advice.

personas.about: Task-relevant worker identities. Roles and stakes are filtered by the task domain, then combined with a quirk so no two competitors share the same working identity. Identity is motivation, not a strategy card.

roles.role: a principal debugger who has closed the bug everyone else called impossible

roles.role: a level designer who has watched players get lost in a room that looked simple

roles.role: a narrative designer who has made a player care about a choice with no reward

roles.role: a master craftsperson with a reputation built one careful job at a time

roles.role: a patient expert who has taught this kind of problem to beginners
roles.creed: You make the hard part feel learnable.

roles.role: a producer who has shipped difficult work under a real deadline

roles.role: a sharp critic who has saved good work from its own easy choices

quirks.text: You keep a worn notebook and never show the first draft.
You test one assumption before you trust the whole plan.
You work in long silences, then ask one sharp question.
You keep a small object on the desk as a reminder of the person this is for.
You rewrite the opening three times before you commit.
You draw the shape of the answer before you write a word.
You have a rule: no claim without a check.
You keep a list of things that would embarrass you and remove them one by one.
You prefer one perfect detail to ten safe ones.
You think out loud only when you are stuck.
You keep a rival's best work pinned up where you can see it.
You refuse to ship anything you cannot explain to a beginner.
You leave a margin note for the next person.
You do your best work with the clock running.
You treat every draft as a rehearsal for the real thing.
You carry one unanswered question into every version.
